picks.rationale: Continuing the bevacizumab maintenance she already tolerates is the lowest-regret choice while the HRD and somatic-BRCA assay is still out. GOG-218 and ICON7 give this regimen more than a decade of post-approval safety data in her exact 1L indication, with hypertension (G>=2 about 22.9% in GOG-218) as the dominant and well-managed toxicity and no marrow or neuropathic signal that touches her stated vetoes. The PFS gain is modest (HR 0.717, no ITT OS benefit), and her VTE history plus prior IVC filter keep bleeding and thrombosis on the monitoring list, but that risk is already accepted in her current plan.
primary_concerns: Bleeding and thrombotic risk on an anti-VEGF agent given her high-VTE history and prior IVC filter, though this risk is already part of her current regimen
Modest PFS benefit with no ITT overall-survival gain on final analysis; the survival signal in ICON7 was confined to the high-risk subgroup

picks.rationale: Niraparib is the one PARP option with a PRIMA benefit across the all-comers ITT (HR 0.62), so it does not strictly wait on the pending HRD score the way SOLO1 and PAOLA-1 do. I rank it second rather than first because its G>=3 anemia (31%) and thrombocytopenia (28.7%) on the fixed starting dose sit squarely against her myelosuppression veto. The individualized starting dose by weight and platelet count is the mitigation that keeps it on the table, and the magnitude sharpens to HR 0.43 if the pending genomic-instability score comes back positive.
primary_concerns: G>=3 anemia 31% and thrombocytopenia 28.7% on the fixed 300 mg start engage her severe-myelosuppression veto; the individualized starting dose is the prerequisite mitigation
Cumulative G>=3 thrombocytopenia rose to 39.7% in the 3.5-year update, so ongoing count monitoring is required across the maintenance window

picks.rationale: For a 70-79-year-old who wants oral, low-burden therapy, letrozole fits her ER-positive high-grade serous biology with none of the marrow or neuropathic toxicity her vetoes name; the class effects are hot flushes, arthralgia, and fatigue with established management. I keep it at rank 3 because the supporting evidence is a single non-randomized cohort (tier 4, ROBINS-I serious, 60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months, p=0.035), not the RCT base behind bevacizumab and the PARP options. Her PR-negativity also tempers the expected endocrine magnitude, so I read this as a low-toxicity holding option rather than a primary maintenance backbone.
primary_concerns: Evidence base is a single non-randomized cohort (tier 4, ROBINS-I serious); no RCT-grade support for maintenance efficacy
PR-negativity and the weak-to-moderate ER intensity temper the expected magnitude of endocrine benefit

notes: Rank order is deliberately gated on the pending tumor HRD and somatic-BRCA result. If that assay returns HRD-positive or shows a somatic BRCA mutation, my view shifts toward an HRD-gated PARP strategy (olaparib + bevacizumab per PAOLA-1, or olaparib per SOLO1 if somatic BRCA-mutated), though I would still weigh the added bleeding/VTE load of stacking a PARP inhibitor onto ongoing bevacizumab against her IVC-filter history. Until the score returns, the safest defensible position is to continue the already-tolerated bevacizumab and hold the PARP decision. I am flagging niraparib's myelosuppression profile and any PARP-plus-bevacizumab stack as candidates for a round-2 toxicity dissent or veto if another persona ranks them first without naming the dose mitigation or the bleeding caution.
